title: Recording lamb weights and growth rates
subtitle: Weighing and tracking lambs from birth to weaning to identify problems early.
excerpt: Regular weighing of lambs from birth to weaning gives an early warning of problems that the eye alone will not catch: a lamb growing slowly usually has an underlying issue, from a low-yielding ewe to a subclinical gut problem. A simple record of birth weight, weaning weight, and target daily gain is enough to flag any animal falling behind the rest of the group.
sourceNotes: AHDB Beef and Lamb, Better Returns Programme: Sheep BRP Manual (2022), sections on lamb performance. Moredun Research Institute, Lamb performance recording (2021). DEFRA, Animal Recording and Movement System (ARAMS) guidance for sheep keepers (2023). SAC Consulting, Lamb growth targets for UK breeds (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: The average weight a lamb gains per day over a given period, calculated as the difference between two weights divided by the number of days between them. A useful summary of how efficiently a lamb is growing.

A lamb's weight at the point it is separated from its mother, typically between 10 and 16 weeks of age depending on the management system. Weaning weight is the key commercial performance indicator in a lamb enterprise.

content.text: Weighing lambs at birth, at four weeks, and at weaning, and comparing those weights against breed targets, is the most practical way to catch problems before they become serious. A lamb with low
daily liveweight gain
is telling you something is wrong: the ewe's milk supply, the pasture, the lamb's gut, or its health. Weight records are not bureaucracy; they are early warning.
What you need

A livestock weighing device: a small hanging scale and a weigh bag or crate works for lambs. A set of dial scales with a cradle is easier for repeated weighing; a portable electronic weigh crate is ideal if you have several ewes.
A notebook or smartphone app for recording. Simple columns: lamb ear tag number, birth date, birth weight, four-week weight, weaning weight.
Ear tags already fitted (required by UK law before lambs leave the holding, and recommended at birth for record-keeping).
Birth weight

Weigh lambs within the first four hours of life, before they have suckled heavily. Typical birth weights for UK commercial ewes (Mule, Texel cross, Suffolk cross) run from 3.5 to 5.5 kg for singles, 2.5 to 4 kg for twins. A lamb under 2.5 kg is at significantly higher risk of hypothermia and colostrum deficiency in the first 24 hours.
Four-week weight
Weigh the lamb at four weeks to the day where possible. The target
daily liveweight gain

from birth to four weeks in a well-managed UK lowland lamb is 250 to 350 g per day. A single lamb on a good ewe will often reach the top of that range. A twin lamb on a moderate ewe may be at 200 g per day, which is acceptable. A lamb at 150 g per day or below needs investigation.
Weaning weight
Record the
weaning weight

on weaning day. Lowland commercial lambs at 14 to 16 weeks typically weigh 28 to 36 kg before going to the finisher field or directly to the abattoir. Work back from your target slaughter weight and weaning date to judge whether growth rates are on track.
Using the data

Flag any lamb with less than 200 g per day gain from birth to four weeks. Check the ewe's milk supply (feel the udder: it should be warm, full, and even on both sides), check the lamb's droppings (loose yellow scour is a gut problem), and check the lamb is actually suckling.
Use birth and weaning weights across your whole lambing to compare ewe productivity. Which ewes consistently produce the heaviest weaners? Those are the replacement females to retain.
Keep records for at least three years. Year-on-year comparisons show whether you are improving, and whether a bad year was a management problem or a weather anomaly.

attrs.cue: Lamb weights are all consistently low compared to breed targets
attrs.cause: Ewe nutrition in late pregnancy, pasture quality, or a flock-wide health issue
attrs.fix: Look at the ewes first. Body condition score at lambing should be 2.5 to 3 on the 1 to 5 scale. Thin ewes produce less colostrum and less milk regardless of the lamb's potential. Review the pre-lambing ration for next year.

attrs.cue: Twins consistently 20% lighter than singles at weaning
attrs.cause: Normal if ewe milk supply is split equally, but significant if one twin is consistently left behind
attrs.fix: This is normal variation. Identify consistently large-weight-discrepancy twin pairs and consider supplementary milk for the smaller twin from two weeks of age if the gap exceeds 30%.
